messages.author: 223747e8d19f24a3
messages.subject: Multiple groups comparison
parts:
Hi,

I have a single IV ('Group') with 3 values - they're arguably categorical or ordinal.  Group has three conditions, C G S, where predicted effect on DVs is C < G < S.
 
I have 11 DVs, all continuous variables.  

I originally was using MANOVA to test the difference between groups, but our local stats guru suggested using path modeling via lavaan instead.  

There aren't any latent variables specified, just one manifest exogenous variable and then the 11 endogenous ones.  The model I have runs just fine, but it's with Group set as an ordinal variables with C G S converted to 0 1 2.  That output shows me that there's a significant change in my endogenous variables as Group 'increases' (ie. goes from C to G to S), but I don't know how to evaluate the magnitude of the effect of shifting from one Group category to the next.  (Ie. is the significance being driven by the increase from C to G, or from G to S?  And what is happening at each level?)  

I'm not sure if the multiple groups option can help me get traction on this - someone suggested using this argument, but it seems like that's more appropriate to employ when you have the same model that you'd like to test in different samples.  In this case, I'd be changing the actual model - breaking down the exogenous variable into three groups, and then all I'd have to compare would be the covariances between my endogenous variables...which doesn't seem quite right.  

Can anyone help me figure out how to proceed here?  I'm new to lavaan, and also relatively new to SEM/path modeling.  Data, model, and syntax attached - thanks in advance!

Andrew

messages.author: 3fe90052fbf2f899
messages.subject: Re: Multiple groups comparison
parts: I originally was using MANOVA to test the difference between groups, but our local stats guru suggested using path modeling via lavaan instead.

Well, the answer depends on what hypotheses you want to test.  If you were original looking at MANOVA, then you might only be interested in comparing the mean vectors across groups.  If that is the case, then this is certainly a decent alternative to MANOVA because you don't have to make the restrictive assumption of sphericity.  Also, MANOVA has differential power to detect group differences in a mean vector depending on the degree and direction of correlation among DVs (e.g., low power when positively correlated, high power when negatively correlated, obviously more complex when you have more than 2 DVs).

There aren't any latent variables specified, just one manifest exogenous variable and then the 11 endogenous ones.  The model I have runs just fine, but it's with Group set as an ordinal variables with C G S converted to 0 1 2.  That output shows me that there's a significant change in my endogenous variables as Group 'increases' (ie. goes from C to G to S), but I don't know how to evaluate the magnitude of the effect of shifting from one Group category to the next.  (Ie. is the significance being driven by the increase from C to G, or from G to S?  And what is happening at each level?)

I would caution against treating your grouping variable as though it were continuous.  You are currently estimating a regression slope for each DV that describes the change in that DV with each unit-increase in the group variable (i.e., identical change between C and G as there is between G and S).  That is a restrictive assumption, and there is no reason to make it.  Graphs of the means show that assumption might be a reasonable for a couple DVs (e.g., wf, we, mf), but you should consider whether you want to make that assumption.

a.data <- read.csv("a_data.csv")
head(a.data)
## save names of dependent variables
DVs <- c("vis.pain","mi","dexterity","wf","we","mf","me","pain","ltd.fxn","swelling","stiffness")

## view mean differences across group to check whether trends are linear
par(mfrow = c(4, 3))
for (i in DVs) {
  myFormula <- as.formula(paste(i, "group", sep = " ~ "))
  groupMeans <- aggregate(myFormula, data = a.data, mean)
  plot(groupMeans)
  lines(groupMeans)
}
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

I'm not sure if the multiple groups option can help me get traction on this - someone suggested using this argument, but it seems like that's more appropriate to employ when you have the same model that you'd like to test in different samples.  In this case, I'd be changing the actual model - breaking down the exogenous variable into three groups, and then all I'd have to compare would be the covariances between my endogenous variables...which doesn't seem quite right.

That's true, but only because you have not included the mean structure in your model.  You can add the mean structure, and test whether the mean vector differs across groups in a multiple-group model.  You can just take the regression out of your current syntax, in which case you are specifying a saturated covariance matrix in each group -- you can also specify a saturated covariance structure pretty quickly/automatically using the code below:

myModel <- outer(DVs, DVs, function(x, y) paste(x, "~~", y))[lower.tri(diag(DVs), diag = TRUE)]
myModel <- paste(myModel, collapse = "\n")
cat(myModel)
## you can specify the saturated mean structure in a lavaan argument (int.ov.free = TRUE)
## or you can specify the saturated mean structure in the syntax:
# myModel <- outer(DVs, DVs, function(x, y) paste(x, "~~", y))[lower.tri(diag(DVs), diag = TRUE)]
# myModel <- paste(c(myModel, paste(DVs, "~", 1, collapse = "\n")), collapse = "\n")
# cat(myModel)

You can then fit that model to your data, but specifying the grouping variable in the "group" argument of your call to the lavaan function:

allFree <- lavaan(myModel, data = a.data, int.ov.free = TRUE, group = "group")

This allows all means to be equal across group, and because it is saturated, the chi-squared fit statistic is 0 (no constraints means no hypotheses to test).  Any null hypotheses you want to test simply requires you to make those constraints.  For instance, the omnibus MANOVA test that the mean vector is equal in all groups can be specified using the "group.equal" argument:

omniFit <- lavaan(myModel, data = a.data, int.ov.free = TRUE, group = "group", group.equal = "intercepts")
## chi-square test of significance rejects that null hypothesis, so group differences exist
inspect(omniFit, "fit")[c("chisq", "df", "pvalue")]

Any follow-up tests require specifying the mean structure directly in your syntax using labels to constrain a specific parameter across specific groups.  I attached a lavaan script showing an example of follow-up tests (analogous to MANOVA, as I would conduct them) for one DV.  I hope it helps.  Let me know if you have questions about it.
 
Terry
